item.title: Stop Pushing Yourself and Let Your Vision Pull You
item.description:
Motivation

Stop Pushing Yourself and Let Your Vision Pull You

Knowing where we’re going motivates us much more than a sense of urgency.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • The adrenaline of urgency can give us a burst of energy, but it burns out quickly.
  • Research suggests that visualizing attaining our goals helps us make progress toward them.
  • Simply wanting a specific outcome is far less effective than truly visualizing its actualization.

One of the most difficult tasks a psychologist takes on is getting a client to slow down. For many of my patients, once they’ve been worked up into a frenzy, the last thing they want to do is take an extra moment to reflect on their situation. Their sense of urgency presses them forward, telling them there’s no time. They have to act now.

Over time, we can start to misconstrue this feeling as necessary to move us to action. But urgency born from the mindset of emergency and true motivation aren’t the same thing.

Vision pulls us forward: The case of Sarah

My client Sarah came to me deeply frustrated. She was facing what she perceived as a crisis of motivation from the team she led. Her company had finally landed fresh funding after a long and arduous fundraising period, and she felt that her colleagues had all lost their sense of urgency.

“We don’t have time to mess around,” Sarah told me, sitting forward in her chair.

I then asked her a question, “Would you rather have a sense of urgency or passionate engagement from your team right now?”

At first, she wasn’t sure what the difference was.

So, I asked Sarah to think about times she had experienced urgency. She described moving quickly, working hard, making difficult trade-offs, and feeling the activation of the fight-or-flight response.

Then I asked Sarah to remember times when she had experienced passionate engagement. This time, she described excitement and enthusiasm. People pulling together, co-creating, enjoying the hard work, and genuinely caring about what they were trying to accomplish.

Suddenly, Sarah looked at me, a new resolve in her eyes. “I guess I really want passionate engagement,” she said, rather than “a bunch of people running around frantically without a shared vision or focus.”

Urgency has its place. But most meaningful goals require us to sustain effort over time. To do that, it helps to have something pulling us forward—a future calling us and asking to be born.

Of course, this principle extends far beyond the workplace. Think about any area of your life where you feel stuck or dissatisfied. If your home has become overwhelmingly cluttered, you could spend a frantic weekend trying to clean every corner, or you could find inspiration by first picturing a calm, organized, and welcoming space.

If you’re looking for a romantic partner, instead of focusing solely on how many dates you can go on, imagine the relationship you hope to create. How do you feel around this person? How do you spend your time together?

Picture this

Our vision of the way the world could be—one year, one month, or even one minute from now—is what underlies every single action we ever take. For many of my clients, developing a strong sense of vision not only offers motivation itself, but also imbues them with stamina, confidence, and meaning.

In our session, I asked Sarah to close her eyes and imagine her company one, three, and five years from now. Then I asked her to picture herself five years in the future, standing in front of her employees and announcing everything they had accomplished. As she did, she reported to me that there was “a lot of energy flowing like electricity through my body.”

Sarah later led her team through a similar exercise. Together, they imagined millions of people being impacted by their work. Afterwards, the team left with an idea not just of what they did, but why.

Research reveals: How visualization works

Research on mental imagery suggests that imagining an experience can activate some of the same neural systems involved in actually perceiving or performing it.[i] That’s one reason visualization has long been incorporated into athletic training. A gymnast might mentally rehearse a routine, or a golfer picture the trajectory of a ball before taking a swing.

A particularly interesting study followed university students and found that vividness of the future self positively predicted subsequent goal achievement.[ii] According to the data, simply feeling positively about one's future self did not show the same relationship, suggesting that being able to picture the future vividly may matter.

In another study, researchers found that envisioning the outcomes of your goals can increase motivation to pursue them, in part because the vision generates positive emotions.[iii] It would seem that imagining a world we genuinely want gives us both a destination and the fuel to reach it.

Your turn: What pulls and what pushes you?

The next time you feel a sense of urgency pushing you forward, ask yourself what’s on the other side of it. What are you actually trying to create? What is it that you would love to see?

Take a moment to picture yourself after the crisis has passed or the goal has been reached. Where are you? What has changed? Who is there with you? What does success look and feel like? Try to make that mental image as vivid and specific as possible.

Remember: our most meaningful goals often take much more than just short bursts of energy. We need to be putting in energy long after adrenaline and anxiety have worn off.

Urgency can spring us into action, but vision sustains us, making the journey forward more meaningful and enjoyable.

item.title: The Strengths Introverts Bring to Work
item.description:
Introversion

The Strengths Introverts Bring to Work

Get fueled by research about how introverts think, contribute, and lead.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Introverts often prefer time to reflect before responding, which can deepen their contributions.
  • Small behavioral shifts can increase an introvert’s visibility.
  • Meeting agendas and individual brainstorming can help reflective thinkers contribute their best ideas.
Lead With Quiet Confidence book jacket.
Source: Jennifer Marcou, used with permission

I’ve been studying, writing about, and coaching introverts for years, yet the more I learn, the more I find to chew on. Many of us introverts prefer fewer words, but there’s no shortage of things to say about us.

Jennifer Marcou brings an especially useful lens: years as a senior corporate executive, paired with her work as a leadership coach and author of Lead With Quiet Confidence: A Practical Guide to Success for Introverts. I asked her what research can tell us about how introverts are wired, what workplaces still get wrong, and how we can make our strengths more visible while staying true to ourselves.

NA: I lose track of time while writing or having meaningful conversations, yet feel drained by cocktail parties. What does research show about how introverts and extroverts experience their surroundings differently?

JM: Introversion and extroversion influence how people gain energy and respond to stimulation. Introverts are often energized by reflection, solitude, and meaningful conversations, while extroverts gain energy through interaction.

Research suggests introverts generally prefer lower levels of stimulation and process information internally before responding. Introverted brains tend to be rewarded by acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter associated with calm, focused thinking and reflection. Extroverts are often more comfortable thinking out loud and refining ideas through discussion. Extroverted brains are often rewarded by dopamine, a neurotransmitter that is linked to engagement, excitement, and social interaction.

This helps explain why introverts may thrive in deep work or reflection yet feel drained by highly stimulating environments. The same characteristics can support strengths such as deep thinking, careful listening, preparation, and thoughtful decision-making. Neither style is better. They are simply different ways of engaging with the world.

NA: As an introvert, I prefer to listen, reflect, and fully form a thought before I share it, but fast-moving meetings can make it difficult to contribute. I’ve learned to navigate that by preparing key points beforehand, connecting with people one-on-one, and following up afterward. From your experience as a senior executive, how can introverts play to their strengths while ensuring their ideas are heard?

JM: Congratulations on finding these strategies of preparation, connecting one-on-one, and following up. Introverts often generate insight through reflection, but organizations frequently reward the fastest contributors before the deepest thinkers. Another effective strategy is asking thoughtful questions such as, “What are we missing?” or “What does success look like?” Strong questions can be just as influential as strong answers.

I also encourage introverts to contribute within the first ten minutes of a meeting. Preparing one or two points in advance helps ensure their perspective becomes part of the discussion. The goal is not to speak more. It is to get your thinking heard. Confidence often follows contribution.

NA: What misconceptions about introverts have you encountered most often in corporate leadership, and how can they affect their careers?

JM: One of the biggest misconceptions is that quiet people have less to contribute. Because introverts tend to listen and reflect before speaking, they can be perceived as lacking confidence or leadership potential when the opposite is often true.

These assumptions can limit visibility and opportunities. Early in my career, a colleague jokingly called me the “Ice Queen” because I rarely smiled or initiated conversations. To change that perception, I made a point of greeting five people each morning. Colleagues noted that I became more approachable.

The lesson was not that I needed to change my personality. I simply changed one behavior. Small visible actions can help others experience the real you without compromising authenticity.

NA: Your LEAD framework—learn, experiment, assess, develop—encourages introverts to try new behaviors while remaining authentic. How have you seen it help people grow?

JM: One client dreaded leading project meetings because she believed leaders needed all the answers. Through coaching, she realized her strength was asking thoughtful questions rather than providing every solution.

That experience inspired my LEAD framework. First, identify what you want to learn. Next, run a small behavioral experiment. Then assess what worked and what you learned. Finally, continue developing the skill.

The client discovered that her questions improved decision-making and increased her confidence. Confidence rarely comes before action. It develops through action and experience.

NA: Most leaders manage a mix of personalities. How can understanding introversion and extroversion help bring out the best in both?

JM: Understanding introversion and extroversion is not about labeling people. It is about creating conditions in which different thinking styles can contribute.

Leaders can help by sharing meeting agendas in advance, allowing colleagues time to prepare. They can structure brainstorming sessions so individuals generate ideas independently before group discussion. They can also invite input after meetings, since many people produce their best ideas through reflection.

These simple practices help ensure organizations benefit from both immediate and thoughtful contributions.

Colleagues at meetings.
Source: AI-generated

NA: What would you most like readers to know about succeeding as an introvert at work?

JM: The most important thing to know is that success does not require becoming someone else. Introverts do not need to change their personality to lead effectively.

What matters is behavioral flexibility. You can learn to speak up, build visibility, and expand your influence while remaining authentic. Visibility is not self-promotion. It is ensuring your ideas can benefit others.

Introversion is not a limitation. Qualities such as listening, preparation, reflection, empathy, and deep thinking are leadership strengths. The introverts who make the greatest impact are the ones who take small steps outside their comfort zone and allow others to see the strengths they already possess.

NA: I find the distinction between personality and behavior striking. Jennifer and I both advocate for honoring how introverts are wired while expanding how we operate. That might mean preparing a point before a meeting, asking the question no one else has asked, or simply saying hello to five colleagues. Small shifts can make our strengths easier for others to see. Workplaces benefit, too, when they make room for people who think before they speak as well as those who think out loud.

item.title: When Dyslexia Was Called 'Word Blindness'
item.description:
Cognition

When Dyslexia Was Called 'Word Blindness'

The fascinating history behind our understanding of dyslexia.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Dyslexia was once called “word blindness,” even though vision was never the problem.
  • A young boy’s unusual reading difficulties helped doctors recognize that dyslexia is not about intelligence.
  • Reading is more than seeing. It requires the brain to turn letters into sounds, language, and meaning.

October is Dyslexia Awareness Month, making it a good time to revisit an intriguing chapter in the history of language and the brain: how the medical profession came to understand dyslexia. What began as a puzzling disconnect between vision and reading would eventually reveal that reading is far more than simply seeing words on a page.

A Problem With Written Words, Not Eyes

In the 19th century, doctors encountered people who could speak, write, and understand language normally, yet struggled to read. In the 1870s, German physician Adolf Kussmaul gave this puzzling condition an evocative name: Wortblindheit, or “word blindness” (Stollznow, 2026).

However, the label was misleading. These people were not literally blind, and their eyesight was often perfectly normal. Their difficulty was with the written word. The mystery was how someone could see a word clearly yet be unable to make sense of it.

Kussmaul’s observations influenced Rudolf Berlin, a German ophthalmologist who studied patients struggling to read despite having normal vision. In 1877, Berlin coined a new term for the condition: dyslexia, from Greek roots meaning “difficulty with words.” The new term shifted attention away from blindness and toward the relationship between the brain and written language.

A Bright Boy Who Couldn’t Read

Let’s look at the case of Percy, a 14-year-old English boy described by physician William Pringle Morgan in 1896. Percy was, Morgan observed, “bright and intelligent, quick at games, and in no way inferior to others of his age” (Kirby & Snowling, 2022). Yet he could not learn to read. Percy’s spelling was particularly inventive. He wrote “scone” for song, “scojock” for subject, “wiehout” for without, and even misspelled his own name as “Precy.”

Morgan suspected that Percy’s difficulty was a congenital defect. In modern terms, developmental dyslexia usually begins in childhood and has a strong genetic component. It can run in families, although having a parent with dyslexia does not mean a child will necessarily develop it.

What stands out about Percy’s story is how clearly Morgan distinguished his reading difficulty from his abilities in other areas. Percy’s problem was not a lack of capacity or effort, but the specific challenge of making sense of written language. More than a century later, that distinction remains very important. Dyslexia is a difficulty with reading and language processing, not a measure of intelligence.

When Reading Happens Differently

Today, researchers understand dyslexia as involving differences in how the brain processes written language, particularly the processing of sounds. One core difficulty is phonological awareness: recognizing, separating, and manipulating the sounds that make up words, and connecting those sounds with letters. That can make reading surprisingly effortful. A person with dyslexia may read slowly, misread words, struggle with spelling, or have difficulty distinguishing letters and sounds. Words may seem to blur together, and reading silently can be especially challenging.

But dyslexia does not mean that someone has trouble understanding language. In fact, some people with dyslexia find that they understand and remember information more easily when they hear it rather than read it. This is one reason audiobooks, text-to-speech software, and other tools can make such a difference.

Brain imaging studies have also found differences in the neural networks involved in reading. Typical readers rely heavily on a network of language-related regions, particularly in the left hemisphere. In people with dyslexia, these networks can function differently, with changes in brain activity and connectivity that may make reading more laborious (Carneiro et al., 2024).

Seeing Isn’t the Same as Reading

Dyslexia is surprisingly common. Estimates vary considerably depending on how dyslexia is defined and identified. One recent study of children in elementary school found a pooled prevalence of about 7 percent worldwide (Yang et al., 2022). Some estimates are even higher.

So “word blindness” was not quite the right description. People with dyslexia are not blind to words. Their eyes can see them. Their brains process the relationship between letters, sounds, and language differently.

There is another condition called “word blindness” too, a term once used for acquired difficulties with reading, particularly after brain injury. The medical term alexia is now more commonly used for this condition.

Yet the outdated phrase captures something worth remembering. For someone struggling to read, words can become strangely inaccessible, even when everything else about their vision is working perfectly. The words are there, but seeing them is not the same as reading them.

And perhaps that is what the history of dyslexia teaches us most clearly: The same page can present a very different experience to different brains. A difficulty that once seemed mysterious is now helping us understand just how much happens between seeing a word and making sense of it.

item.title: Do You Make Hair Inferences?
item.description:
First Impressions

Do You Make Hair Inferences?

Hair can shape our perceptions of power, personality, and professionalism.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Professional appearance judgments can disadvantage Black women with natural hairstyles.
  • Gray hair affects perceived age but not necessarily trust or status judgments.
  • People with shaved heads are perceived as stronger and more dominant.
Source: mimagephotography / Shutterstock

You see a man with a shaved head. A woman with gray hair. A Black woman wearing her hair naturally. Someone with long blond hair.

Before any of them speaks, you may already have formed an impression.

Hair is one of the most visible parts of a person’s appearance. We may use it to make inferences that extend far beyond hairstyle. Research suggests that hair can influence our judgments about age and attractiveness, but also dominance, competence, professionalism, health, and personality.

Hair and Power

A particularly revealing study published this year visually separated hair from the face to see how much each contributed to first impressions. Swanson and colleagues (2026) showed participants photographs of 40 people in three different forms: the whole person’s head, the face with the hair hidden, or the hair with the face hidden. Participants were asked to make judgments on either how powerful or warm the person seemed.

Hair turned out to matter quite a lot for judgments of power. Ratings based on the hair alone strongly predicted how powerful the whole person appeared, even after researchers accounted for judgments based on the face. Hair contributed much less to impressions of warmth, such as whether someone seemed kind or cooperative. This research did not attempt to identify which hairstyles made people seem more powerful, however.

But earlier research found a similar effect with shaved heads. Mannes (2013) showed that men with shaved heads were perceived as more dominant than men with full heads of hair. In one experiment, researchers digitally removed the hair from photographs of the same men. The shaved versions were judged as more dominant, taller, and stronger.

So it seems that hair can clearly contribute to impressions of status and physical presence before we know anything about how a person actually behaves.

Hair and Professionalism

The stakes can become higher when judgments of appearance contribute to hiring decisions. Koval and Rosette (2021) examined how Black and White women were evaluated as job candidates while wearing either natural or straightened hairstyles. Across four studies, Black women with natural hairstyles were judged as less professional and less competent than Black women with straightened hair. They were also less likely to be recommended for an interview.

The effect was stronger in industries with relatively conservative appearance norms. In this case, Hair was not simply influencing judgments of attractiveness. Evaluators use the appearance of a candidate's hair to judge whether they looked as though they belonged in a professional role. The distinction matters because standards of “professional appearance” can feel neutral and objective even when they clearly reflect culturally specific expectations about what competent people are supposed to look like.

How Gray Hair Is Perceived

Hair also gives us an immediate cue to age. Nutt and colleagues (2025) digitally altered photographs so that the same faces appeared with gray or non-gray hair. Both men and women were judged as older and less attractive when their hair was gray. Some judgments differed depending on who was doing the observation and rating. Male participant observers rated people with gray hair as less trustworthy, while female participant observers did not. In this study, gray hair didn’t significantly change judgments of social status or aggression.

The pattern is interesting because gray hair changed some impressions while leaving others relatively stable. Hair doesn’t seem to produce one general positive or negative impression. Different characteristics seem to cue different assumptions.

Hair Color and Personality

Hair color can also affect judgments that have little obvious connection to hair. For instance, Swami and Barrett (2011) studied men’s responses to the same woman presented with different hair colors. In a nightclub setting, men approached her more often when she was blond. But when another group of men rated photographs of her, the brunette version was judged as more attractive, intelligent, approachable, and competent. The blond version was also rated as more needy.

Matz and Hinsz (2018) likewise found that women’s hair color and length influenced judgments about age, health, attractiveness, relationship potential, and perceived parenting capability. In their study, lighter hair was generally associated with greater youth, health, and attractiveness.

Could Some Hair Inferences Be Right?

Not every inference from appearance is necessarily wrong. People choose hairstyles for reasons, and their choices can reflect preferences, identity, or even aspects of personality.

In one study of 308 young women, those with short hair scored somewhat higher on fun-seeking, while women who dyed their hair scored higher on extraversion, openness, and emotional stability (Seo & Jeong, 2009). But the overall relationships between hairstyle and personality were weak, and hairstyle explained very little of the variation in personality.

Broader research on first impressions suggests that people can sometimes make above-chance personality judgments from appearance. Naumann and colleagues (2009), for example, found that observers viewing full-body photographs could judge traits such as extraversion with some accuracy, partly because appearance contains cues people choose, like clothing and grooming, as well as expressive cues such as posture and facial expression.

So a hairstyle may occasionally tell you something real about the person who chose it. The problem is when we over-interpret what we are seeing. Hair can provide a clue, but it’s a very small sample of evidence from which to infer an entire personality. In fact, although many people take great pride in their appearance, especially their hair, some of its characteristics are not easy to alter. Ethnicity, gender, and age are common factors that determine the appearance of our hair and have little to do with personality.

From Hair to Person

Yet, hair matters because it’s highly visible, changeable, and often specifically chosen. A haircut, color, texture, or decision to let hair turn gray can alter the impression we make before we even say a word.

That’s what makes hair inferences interesting. We notice a real cue and build a larger picture of the person from it. Sometimes that picture may be partly accurate. Sometimes it reflects stereotype or expectation. The next time you form an immediate impression of someone, it may be worth asking how much of it came from the actual person and how much came from their hair.

item.title: Why Is It So Hard to Let Go?
item.description:
Spirituality

Why Is It So Hard to Let Go?

The challenge of learning to live in the present.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Holding on keeps us stuck in the past.
  • Dwelling on what happened prolongs our anger, hurt, and frustration.
  • Letting go means accepting what has already happened.
  • Releasing the past frees us to meet the next moment as a new moment.

The other day I asked a bus driver when her bus was leaving. She was sitting in the driver’s seat eating a sandwich. “I'm on my break,” she said. “Look at the schedule!” She sounded annoyed. I apologized for interrupting her break. "Look at the schedule!" she said again, emphatically. The annoyance had a swipe of anger.

It would have been so easy for her to say, “Five minutes,” or “Ten minutes,” or whatever the answer was. Instead, she spent more time being irritated. I got pulled into her emotional riptide. I felt upset.

I caught a different bus on a different line. The second driver waited patiently while I loaded my bicycle onto the front of the bus. But once I was sitting on the bus, I kept thinking about the first driver. In my head I was running through everything I wanted to say to her: What’s wrong with you? Why couldn’t you just answer the question? Why is it so hard to be a little bit nice? I was still angry.

Here I was, already on another bus, well on my way, with a driver who had been nice, but I was still in the past, on the first bus. Why is it so hard to let go?

We Hold On for Dear Life

The Buddha said human suffering has three causes: clinging, aversion, and ignorance.

Clinging: We want things to be a certain way. Aversion: We don’t want things to be a certain way. Ignorance: We don’t understand that nothing is permanent.

Everything is changing. Everything is in constant transformation. Every moment is a new moment. Every breath is a new breath. Yet we hold on for dear life.

We hold on because we think everything is ours. My body. My house. My work. My relationship. My children. My life. But what if this life isn’t something we own? What if we are part of this life?

We are part of nature. Everything in nature grows from a seed, develops, matures, and then returns to nature. Constant transformation. It's hard for us to let go because we identify with the physical world without realizing it's always changing. We hold on mostly out of fear.

What Happens When We Can’t Let Go?

Today I heard that a former student at the high school where I’m consulting had attempted suicide. One of his teachers, whom I’m training as a performance specialist, was deeply shaken.

She immediately began looking backward. What could I have done last year? How could I have helped him? Should I have known? These are understandable questions. When something terrible happens, the mind wants to go backward and change what has already occurred. But we can’t.

A close cousin of mine called to tell me that her dear friend, who's terminally ill, chose to end his life through assisted suicide. How difficult this was for everyone who loved him and didn’t want him to die. They wanted him to stay. He chose to go.

How do we let go of someone we love when we don’t want to let go? Here again is the challenge of moving into the ever-unfolding present instead of holding on to something, or someone, who has passed.

This is the great challenge of life: to live in the present moment. To accept what is without wishing it were different. Acceptance doesn’t mean that we don’t care or that we don’t act. It means accepting what is going on right now and asking: What now? Not: Why did this happen? Not: Why didn’t I do something differently? Instead, we should be asking: What now?

Learning to Swim in the Ocean of Life

If learning to let go, accept change, and stay in the present is among life's great challenges, where are we supposed to learn how to do that?

We’re never taught this stuff. We’re never taught how to swim in life's ocean. We are taught so many peripheral things: trigonometry, history, DNA. We spend years looking at the way things work without learning how to deal with what life actually brings us.

How do you deal with disappointment? With loss? With fear? How do you let go of someone you love who dies? How do you stay present when everything inside you wants the present moment to be different?

We teach young people how to pass tests without teaching them how to meet the tests that life itself will give them. We need a revolution in our teaching and in how we prepare people for life.

There Is Nothing to Hold On To

Stress is a function of disconnection from the present moment, from ourselves, from other people, and from what matters most.

The first bus driver was gone. The bus was gone. The interaction was over. But I was still carrying it. I was dealing with what had already happened and wishing it had happened differently.

Clinging. Aversion. Ignorance.

And then there was another bus. Another driver. Another moment. Life had already moved on. The question was whether I was willing to move with it.

Maybe that is what letting go really means. Not pushing something away. Not pretending it didn’t happen. Not denying grief, anger, disappointment, or fear.

It means coming back to what is here. This breath. This person. This challenge. This moment.

We don’t own any of it. Instead, we are part of it.

There is nothing to hold on to and everything to gain.

We give our lives to service. We accept. We grow. We serve.

Coda

Just before I submitted this post, I stopped at a local store. The lit sign in the window said OPEN, but when I tried the door, the shopkeeper said, “We’re not open yet.”

I pointed out that the OPEN sign was lit. “I’m turning it off," he said angrily. "We're not open."

Rather than argue, I left but immediately started thinking about all the nasty, angry things I wanted to say to him. Just like the bus driver.

But this time I caught it fast. I exhaled. I felt my feet on the ground.

The sun was bright. A new moment.

item.title: Surprising Ingredients for Beating Loneliness
item.description:
Loneliness

Surprising Ingredients for Beating Loneliness

Difference and disconnection can actually promote healthy relationships.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Friction and disconnection are essential ingredients to healthy development and relationships.
  • People need to embrace opportunities for unexpected connection with those who are different from them.
  • Professionals can look to mutual recognition for a detailed framework on how difference promotes good therapy.

We are living in an age of widespread loneliness and disconnection. To make matters more complicated, encountering difference very often quickly transforms into fear, threat, and various self-protective responses which, by definition, increase distance rather than foster connection.

Such fear responses have their place, and there are many scenarios where distancing ourselves from perceived threat is indeed the appropriate and adaptive response. The problem is when these responses are activated at such a low threshold that any whiff of difference or friction is experienced the same as real danger, creating a different kind of danger—isolation and quietly devastating loneliness.

Although I am quick to point out the limitations of insight, in this case, a bit of grounded education may be an entryway to softening some automatic reactions to encountering difference.

In short: Learning to relate with others who are experienced as different from ourselves is an essential ingredient to feeling deeply connected.

Rupture and repair

Leaders in attachment and mentalization research have conducted incredible studies on infant-caregiver interactions and learned that optimally safe, secure, caring, and growth-producing relationships are those which are not perfectly attuned with flawless mirroring at all times, but rather, relationships that engage a dance of connection, disconnection, and reconnection. The tolerable flaws, empathic “misses,” and moments of discomfort or inattention which are followed by the joy and relief of restored connection are what promote the development of self-esteem, self-agency, and trust in oneself and others.

Alternatively, those who have not been fortunate to experience this dance in early development may find everyday moments of disconnection, difference, or disagreement intolerable, and even minor conflicts can escalate into all-out arguments or cut-off relationships. The solution is in the problem. If this resonates, ultimately, what is needed is to experience the dance of disconnection and reconnection for yourself. When there are enough cues for safety (for many, this is in a therapeutic relationship), then a person can start to try out this dance, metaphorically stepping on their partner’s toes (and vice versa) and slowly discovering a rhythm that accommodates frustration, disappointment, and misunderstanding without destroying a sense of connection and trust.

For an accessible read on this subject, I recommend the book The Power of Discord by Ed Tronick, MD, and Claudia Gold, MD.

The power of unexpected connection

The “psychotherapeutic hospital” was once a more widely recognized and available option for people in need of psychiatric care beyond stabilization, a place where they could stabilize, yes, but also re-engage with others, restore hope, feel known, and take risks in the company of other people who were seeking the same things.

When I worked at such a hospital, the patients and I would at times lightheartedly describe the phenomenon of rich and unexpected community as akin to “The Breakfast Club.” It was an apt comparison because the patient milieu was indeed a mixed bag. Ages ranging from mid 20s to late 70s, varying issues, life circumstances, SES, physicalities, worldviews, all came together, and the most surprising of bonds were formed. Importantly, it was typically this part of the hospital experience that patients most credited with their relief, recovery, and renewed sense of hope, which was seen as a win by professional staff.

We all would do well to generate more opportunities for unexpected connection in our lives; however, we risk starving ourselves of them if we are only open to connection in the places where we expect to find it. This means being open to connection despite differences (even disagreement) and working to find the bridge that connects two humans in a shared experience (Shapiro, 2005).

To be clear, this should not be at the risk of one’s safety, physical or emotional. The task of opening oneself to unexpected connection is aided by thoughtful discernment, which is neither naively open nor overconfidently foreclosed.

Experiencing others as distinct and separate

For some, others feel too different from themselves; perhaps they feel alien and like they don’t belong amongst the rest of society. For others, there is a risk of feeling too much the same, even merged, as if they feel what others feel around them without any control or protections, boundary-less. While this may sound romantic in a way, for those who experience it on a regular basis, it is overwhelming, disorienting, and makes it difficult to feel grounded and secure in their own identity and essential boundaries.

If this is relatable, then one aspect of increasing connection with others will be to develop a more distinct, separate, and secure sense of oneself—to be able to know where oneself ends and someone else begins. Often this requires more than self-study or independent personal growth and is best supported by therapy with someone who is experienced in helping those with diffuse identities, loose psychological boundaries, and difficulties with mentalization.

“Sameness and difference exist simultaneously in mutual recognition…things don’t have to be perfect, that, in fact, it is better if they are not… Experiences of ‘being with’ are predicated on a continually evolving awareness of difference, on a sense of intimacy as felt as occurring between ‘the two of us.’” (Benjamin, 1988, p. 47)

Mutual recognition

For the academically inclined and readers with a professional interest in this subject, the concept of mutual recognition within relational psychoanalysis helps to further articulate the role that difference and distinction play in the experience of togetherness. As famously described by Jessica Benjamin, mutual recognition is “a relation in which each person experiences the other as a 'like subject,' another mind who can be 'felt with,' yet has a distinct, separate center of feeling and perception (2004, p. 5).”

In this dynamic, separateness does not threaten connection, but rather allows for a reciprocal relationship. Its counter, complementary relationships, represent a breakdown in mutuality where the involved parties fall into a “doer” and “done-to” interaction, destroying freedom and leading to impasses. The solution is for both/all parties to take mutual responsibility for the dynamic, not retaliating against or submitting to the other, but together surrendering to the reality of separateness, restoring each’s capacities to think creatively and take up self-agency.

Once again, the salve to disconnection and power struggles is to embrace and work with the reality of differences rather than fight against it.

Takeaways

  • Alleviating loneliness involves learning to recognize safe avenues to pursue connection. Restricting one's definition of "safety" to those who are overtly similar not only limits options, but also stifles the development of genuine relational security.
  • If you are trying to learn how to navigate differences and disconnection in relationships, then giving yourself a safe context to practice can help. Find a therapist who works relationally, encourages open communication and curiosity around frustration and disappointment, and try talking about when you want to pull away from that relationship before acting on that feeling.
  • Practice curiosity and nonjudgment when you encounter others who are different from yourself and listen for what can be shared experientially, even if the surface-level details are different. See what happens when you highlight and stay engaged with those pockets of connection.
  • Supporting the development of psychological boundaries supports healthy relationships with others. Feeling separate promotes a feeling of connection.
